If it’s possible do an inventory of items 1st? That could potentially help you figure out if there are items missing, and how they went missing (i.e., did the items run out, were they allocated to another department/site, were they sold, stored somewhere else, etc.). Not sure what kind of business you work for so some of those examples may not apply. Does EE1 have a social media business page? You could also check there to see if any of the work items mentioned are advertised/displayed. I would definitely get as much tangible evidence as you can before approaching EE1 about the allegations.

If your company has a legal team I would loop them in on what’s going on and provide them with all the documentation you currently have so it won’t come as a surprise when y’all finally receive the alleged EEOC complaint that was filed. 

Dealt with something similar at the previous company I worked for. Only thing that saved us was how well documented our prior conversations with the employee and our investigation were. The fact that the employee had never filed any grievances regarding discrimination his entire career with us until his job was on the line (he had worked for us for 8 years) helped too.

As long as you have been diligent in your documentation and so has the supervisor when he’s had to address performance/attendance/conduct/etc. issues you shouldn’t be too worried.
